e3041aa16922ed0adc127eddd975e927.text: Manager of library services Jennifer Coupe speaks at a grand opening celebration for the recently renovated Cariboo Regional District Library Williams Lake Branch on Tuesday, Nov. 10. A prayer at the newly renovated public library in Williams Lake was provided by Williams Lake First Nation elder Virginia Gilbert who was joined with Frances Supernault for drumming and singing. Attending the grand reopening of the Williams Lake public library on Tuesday, Nov. 10 was Williams Lake Mayor Surinderpal Rathor who was joined with councillors Nathan Wiebe, Paul French and Ruth Lloyd. Cariboo Regional District (CRD) chair and Electoral Area H Director Margo Wagner. A fresh new look at the Cariboo Regional District Library in Williams Lake was recently celebrated following two months of renovations. The branch was temporarily closed in September and October with limited services available through outdoor pop-up libraries to allow for repainting in addition to new carpeting, furnishings and circulation desk. It reopened on Tuesday, Nov. 3 with a grand reopening a week later that included Virginia Gilbert and Frances Supernault of the Williams Lake First Nation providing a prayer, drumming and singing. Speeches were additionally shared by officials including Cariboo Regional District (CRD) chair and Electoral Area H Director Margo Wagner and Williams Lake Mayor Surinderpal Rathor. Wagner admitted she is not in the library often although she does access electronic materials. “But the difference from when I was here last time is unbelievable,” she said. “It’s so much brighter, there seems to be more room, there’s more additions that make it more like a living room rather than a library.” Funding for the project was provided by the BC Public Library Enhancement Grant that Manager of Library Services Jennifer Coupe said they had received in 2023. “It took three and half years to get this project off the ground and it was well worth it,” she said, thanking staff for their countless

72977feadac525a3042f3346b85f7b2c.text: Members of various representative groups march along Oliver Street on the way to plaque dedication at City Hall in 1994. The cenotaph was re-dedicated in front of city hall on Nov. 3, 1984. From spectators gathering for a flag-raising at a new Cenotaph in 1968 to veterans marching to city hall for a Korean War plaque dedication in 1994, Williams Lake has a long tradition of honouring those who served – one that continues. The Williams Lake and District Cenotaph was built in 1968 below the former War Memorial Hospital, a joint undertaking by the municipality and Royal Canadian Legion Branch 139 to honour the area’s war dead, according to the Veterans Affairs Canada’s website. The Cariboo War Memorial Hospital opened in May 1925, partly funded by the community of Soda Creek to honour fallen First World War soldiers. In 1968, the _Williams Lake Tribune_ reported on spectators gathering for a flag-raising ceremony at the new monument. Sixteen years later, the cenotaph was moved beside city hall and rededicated on Nov. 3, 1984, in conjunction with the dedication of the new municipal building. Days after the cenotaph’s rededication beside city hall, the _Tribune’s_ Nov. 8, 1984 edition outlined the plans for that year’s Remembrance Day Observance, bringing together veterans, students and community groups. The service began at 10:45 a.m. at the Elks Hall on Nov. 11, 1984 with the Williams Lake Community Band playing O Canada and a student from Anne Stevenson Junior Secondary School’s drama class reading In Flanders Field. Bill Lannigan and A.E McMath read the names of the former residents who died in the First and Second World Wars, followed by the Last Post and two minutes of silence. After the service, Legion members, RCMP, Sea Cadets, Air Cadets and youth organizations included Cubs, Scouts, Voyageurs, Guides and Brownies paraded to the cenotaph for wreath-laying, before returning to the Legion hall to lay wreaths at its cairn. On Thursday, Nov. 5, Prime Minister Mark Carney presented the 2026 federal budget in Parliament. In this extensive budget, Carney has outlined a plan to invest more in the economy and culture of Canada to help address the affordability crisis and the general economic uncertainty gripping the global economy. The budget also calls for constructing more affordable housing and accommodations for the 65,000 Canadians experiencing homelessness. “Investment that builds our sovereignty. Entrepreneurs empowered to grow. Ideas that become companies. Artists who tell our stories. Energy we generate and control. More choices and lower costs for you. A home for every Canadian,” Carney wrote in the budget’s cover letter. “This is what it means to be ‘Maîtres chez nous’. A sovereign Canada, where we take care of each other, where we create opportunities for all, and where we are free to live our lives as we choose.” A member of the Conservative Party, Doherty is critical of the Liberal Government’s budget, pointing specifically to the $765 billion in debt he said it will add to the country’s deficit over the next five years. Doherty said this is the equivalent of $44,000 in debt for every Canadian household. During a time when many Canadians are struggling to pay for groceries, fuel and housing, Doherty believes the country cannot afford a government that spends billions of dollars. He asserted the first goal of this budget should have been saving Canadians money, not putting more debt on their backs. “The fastest-growing item in this budget is interest on the national debt. The Regional District of North Okanagan is working with a local environmental group to assess what can be done about the pond. The City of Vernon’s new council held its first meeting Tuesday, and one of its first orders of business was to receive some worrisome information relating to the area’s water shortages heading into next year. Hayley Dosser, a scientist with the Canadian Centre for Climate Services, made a delegation to Vernon council at its inaugural meeting Nov. 10, to discuss what is expected to be the most intense super El Niño on record, which has been building in the tropical Pacific Ocean since September. An El Niño is a climate pattern that sees higher than average sea surface temperatures in the central and eastern tropical Pacific Ocean create a shift in weather patterns well beyond the Pacific Ocean. A super El Niño is simply an extreme version of this phenomenon. Dosser said the temperature at the ocean’s surface has now passed three degrees Celsius above the baseline, “so we are in a very strong El Niño.” The climate scientist explained that this sets the stage for extreme weather and related impacts, such as were scene in the winters of 1982-83, 1997-98 and 2015-16. While the impacts of an El Niño are generally less severe in Canada compared to other countries, past events are estimated to have cost Canada billions of dollars, Dosser said. “This particular El Niño event is quite exceptional. It is very likely to be unprecedented, potentially by a substantial margin,” she added. In Canada, the strongest direct effects of El Niño on weather tend to occur in winter and spring, Dosser said. “We can see that we tend to have milder and drier winters with less snow. ae26be1308a32457a0321b8f732a9c40.text: B.C. businesswoman receives US$5K NEXUS fine in crackdown | Williams Lake Tribune South Surrey businesswoman Suzanne Smith says she is fighting the recent revocation of her NEXUS pass, as well as the US$5,000 fine she was handed. Suzanne Smith received confirmation of her NEXUS pass revocation in September. A South Surrey woman who operated three boutique stores south of the border for more than a dozen years before closing her last U.S. shop in May says she has been stripped of her trusted-traveller privileges and hit with a US$5,000 fine for violating a rule she never knew existed. Suzanne Smith of Betty Be Good Boutique said Nov. 2 that her experience has made her nervous about future crossings, and that it is a cautionary tale that she hopes others can learn from. “I’m someone who regularly crosses the border who did not know the rules of the game have changed,” said Smith. “I don’t want this to happen to other people, and I also want others to just be on alert if they’re planning to go there.” The incident that triggered the penalties occurred in September, when Smith used her NEXUS pass to cross the border to pick up business and personal parcels from her U.S. post-office box. Driving an empty vehicle, she said she “told the agent exactly why I was going down there, to pick up parcels,” and was waved through without further questions. Heading back to Canada, she encountered a checkpoint in the commercial lane. The border officer asked, “How did you get to America today?” and upon learning it was via the NEXUS lane, peppered Smith with “rapid-fire” questions: did she have a transponder? Had she told the earlier border officer that she was crossing for work? Had she paid the single-crossing fee – currently US$22.10 – required of those crossing into the U.S. for commercial purposes? 8f05f13d0d3df218e6113228dd1bf573.text: The Athabasca Chipewyan First Nation in Alberta is suing British Columbia, the federal government, and BC Hydro for what it says are Treaty 8 rights violations related to several dams on the Peace River, including Site C, now known as the John Horgan Dam. “The Province and British Columbia Hydro built these hydroelectric projects without regard for the rights, culture and way of life of ACFN, which includes the exercise of its Treaty Rights,” the lawsuit, filed on Nov. 5 in B.C. Supreme Court, argues. B.C.’s Ministry of Attorney General declined to comment on the case because the government is in “caretaker mode” following the Oct. 24 election. The incoming government is not due to be sworn in until Nov. 20. The First Nation signed Treaty 8 in 1899, guaranteeing protection for the Chipewyan way of life in exchange for allowing settlement and development in the nation’s territories. When B.C. began building dams along the Peace River, including the W.A.C. Bennnet Dam (completed in 1967), the Peace Canyon Dam (completed in 1980), and finally the Site C Dam (finished in 2024), the nation says the province failed to consult on the impacts on the Peace River Delta. And B.C. is now in the early stages of “information-gathering” on another potential dam on the river at a place known as Site E near the Alberta border. The nation says that BC Hydro did not even speak of the downstream impacts during hearings related to the earlier dams, and did not include the delta area in the environmental assessment area for Site C, claiming there would be “no detectable effects” from Site C. But the Athabasca Chipewyan First Nation says it is experiencing lasting impacts from the dams. The nation blames the dams for altering the river’s natural flow and seasonal timing, impacting water quality and interfering with the area’s natural ecology, which affects fish, wildlife and vegetation. Four bears have been euthanized after being conclusively linked to the killing of a mother and daughter from Bella Coola. ​At a press conference on Tuesday, Nov. 10, BC Conservation Officer Service (BCCOS) Inspector Jeff Tyre confirmed that forensic testing determined that four grizzly bears captured by the BCCOS over the last several days were all actively involved in the attack. ​“Evidence from the investigation as well as animal DNA was analyzed and conclusively linked to a sow and three offspring,” Tyre said. ​Family members have identified the victims as Jennifer Balcarras, 48, and her daughter Selah Reed, 20, who failed to return after going for a walk on the Snooka West Trail on Nov. 1. They were killed in a grizzly bear attack less than a year after several school children and one adult were left with serious injuries. The inspector added that the bears have been dispatched to protect the public after consideration of all the evidence and analysis of provincial human-wildlife conflict response guidelines. “This was a heartbreaking event for the families, the Nuxalk Nation and the Bella Coola community,” Tyre said. “We hope the efforts of everyone who responded, along with these findings, bring some measure of closure. Our thoughts remain with everyone affected.” According to Tyre, the investigation also pointed to likely predatory behaviour, which he stressed is very rare. “We don’t know how it started, but we know how it ended,” he said. The BCCOS inspector added that more than a dozen conservation officers took part in the complex investigation over the past week, working in difficult terrain and weather, while carefully managing ongoing risk to the public and responders involved. The Cabot Revelstoke Mountain Lodge under construction at Revelstoke Mountain Resort on Sept. 16. Green fees have been announced for Revelstoke’s new luxury golf course set to open next summer, though only hotel guests may play for the first season. Bookings for staying and playing at Cabot Revelstoke starting July 2027 have opened, its team announced early this month. The inaugural season for the 18-hole course at Revelstoke Mountain Resort will run July 2 to Sept. 30, but exclusively for golfers staying at the new 155-room Karl Hotel that overlooks the 18th green. For both local and visiting golfers interested in stays, “we’re delighted to extend an exclusive invitation to be among the first to experience this extraordinary destination, with priority access to golf stay-and-play reservations ahead of our broader public launch,” real estate manager Holly Nichols shared on Wednesday, Nov. 4. Golf rates for next year are $315 per round for non-local hotel guests, $225 for local hotel guests, $175 for junior hotel guests age 16 and under, and $175 for PGA members. To stay at the Karl Hotel, standard king rooms (the cheapest accommodation) fit two guests and cost $319. A standard double-queen room with two beds sleeps four guests and costs $399, making it the most affordable per-person option. These rates are subject to taxes and add-ons include sofa beds, balconies and kitchenettes. “Day golf” for players other than hotel guests is not currently available and will be added as an option at a later date, Cabot Revelstoke clarified. For now, Karl Hotel guests who submit a booking request can expect a follow-up from Cabot Revelstoke’s reservations team to confirm availability for stays and golf play. eae930c57c2abf322ad976158a7614e2.text: Prince George RCMP are asking for the public’s help to locate a young child who was reportedly seen running alone along the John Hart Bridge. According to an RCMP press release, police received multiple reports shortly before 6 p.m. on Wednesday, Nov. 6, of an unidentified child running on the roadway near the on-ramp from North Nechako Road to Highway 97 southbound. Mounties said the child was described as female, approximately three to six years old, with purple hair and wearing a green shirt. According to the release, multiple officers immediately attended the area and conducted extensive patrols, including a drone search, but were unable to locate the child. “We believe that the child may have been picked up by a guardian, who has decided not to report the situation,” Sgt. Craig Douglass of the Prince George RCMP said. “We would like to ask the guardian or anyone who knows this child to reach out to us so that we may confirm their well-being.” Police are also asking anyone with additional information or dashcam footage from the area at the time of the incident to come forward. Anyone with information or video footage is asked to contact the Prince George RCMP at 250-561-3300 as soon as possible.

97a62cdc4a3bcd3f6d074fb609892faa.text: Environment Canada has issued multiple yellow and orange warnings all over B.C. for wind and rain Heavy wind and rainfall warnings have been issued all over B.C. Environment Canada has issued multiple yellow and orange warnings, which are active as of Wednesday, Nov. 11. “Drivers are advised to monitor conditions and expect possible areas of pooling water on roadways, fallen debris and the potential for short-notice road closures,” wrote DriveBC. The winds may cause utility outages and turn high-sided vehicles over. “Secure loose objects. If outside, protect yourself from flying or falling debris. Stay away from fallen power lines. Prepare for some disruptions to transportation, services, and utilities,” said Environment Canada. Heavy rainfall may cause water pooling on roads and low-lying areas. Visibility may also be reduced at times. Landslides are likely to occur in vulnerable areas, such as steep slopes, deforested areas or recent burn scars. “Areas expected to be harder hit by the storm include Highway 99 through the Sea to Sky corridor and Pemberton Valley, Highway 1 through the Fraser Valley and the Fraser Canyon, and the Malahat and west coast communities on Vancouver Island,” added DriveBC.

Leroy George holds his Korean War medal in his Chilliwack home on Tuesday, Nov. 10, 2026. The Canoe River train disaster memorial is in Valemount, B.C. In 1950, Leroy George was engaged to a woman named Ruthie, on the promise that he would never join the military. They married on Aug. 7, 1950; within a week, George had enlisted. In November, George was on his way by train from Shiloh, Man. to Fort Lewis, Wash. for training. His train collided with another train on the way. Shortly after, Ruthie George was told her husband was dead. “That was quite a hell of a shock for my young wife at that time,” George said. “We hadn’t been married for not even a month.” George, who served in the Canadian military for 40 years before retiring, told the story of the train crash during a ceremony to honour Indigenous veterans at the K’ómoks First Nation Gym in Courtenay on Friday (Nov. 6). “The second day of the journey, a few of us were playing cards,” George said in a speech during the ceremony. “I wasn’t much interested in the game, so I gave my seat to a young soldier named (Basil) Patrick McKeown. A few minutes after I gave up my seat, we felt a tremendous bump.” Twenty-one people died in the crash, including 17 soldiers, and the crew members of both trains. McKeown and George’s cousin, Austin Emery George, were among the soldiers who were killed. “When we had the train accident, (Ruthie) got a telegram saying I had been deceased. Then a day or so later, after we had a roll call and they brought us back to Wainwright, Alta. to be checked out and re-equipped again, she got another mail saying that I was alive,” George said. He said officials must have either mistaken his cousin or McKeown for him. “We don’t know how they misrepresented me, but we got it cleared up a couple of days later,” George said. 66698c80d397321b3d40b5cc3903de78.text: **By Peter Kvarnstrom, B.C. & Yukon Community News Media Association** Crowds gathered as Conservative Tracy St. Claire won the Penticton-Summerland election race. Incumbent mayoral candidate Nicole MacDonald followed the election results as they came in on Saturday, Oct. 17. British Columbians went to the polls twice in October, electing local councils and school boards just one week before choosing a new provincial government. For local newspapers, that meant covering two elections at once. Their journalists reported on hundreds of candidates, examined promises and helped voters understand the choices before them. Across Black Press community newspapers and eight Glacier Media publications alone, more than 7,000 election stories and columns were published. Nearly 2,800 of those covered municipal elections. That is an extraordinary amount of work by newsrooms that have already endured years of cuts. It was particularly important at the municipal level. Unlike provincial political parties, local candidates have fewer resources to reach voters. They rely heavily on community newspapers to introduce themselves, explain their positions and have their ideas examined. But the coverage we saw this fall raises a troubling question: when British Columbians next go to the polls, how many of those newspapers will still be around to cover the election? Community newspapers have struggled for years as advertising revenue has shifted to large American digital platforms such as Facebook and Google. Newsrooms have become smaller, budgets have tightened, and publishers have had to make difficult decisions about what they can continue to cover. This summer, an already struggling industry was dealt another serious financial blow. TC Transcontinental, one of Canada’s largest producers of retail advertising flyers, began moving major flyer distribution away from local newspapers and into a new delivery system using Canada Post.
